answer.label: Not Fyodor Dostoevsky — an anonymous modern fabrication
answer.authorDates: Circulating online since c. 2019 · falsely attributed to Dostoevsky from 2021
answer.sourceLine: This line appears in none of Dostoevsky’s novels, letters, diaries or notebooks. Fact-checkers at Snopes ↗ and Lead Stories ↗ found no record of him writing it; it began as an anonymous Russian-language meme around 2019 and was pinned to Dostoevsky in English only from mid-2021.

source.heading: What the record actually shows

docMeta.dd: None — no novel, letter, diary or notebook cited

source.excerpt: Tolerance will reach such a level that intelligent people will be banned from thinking so as not to offend the imbeciles.
trail: The quote surfaced as an anonymous Russian-language meme, appearing on Reddit and social media by around 2019, often over a still from the 1988 film of Bulgakov’s Heart of a Dog, per Fakenews.pl ↗.
The English attribution to Dostoevsky spread on Facebook from July 2021, notably among anti-vaccine accounts, according to Lead Stories ↗.
A University of Toronto Slavic-studies reference check confirmed the words appear in neither Bulgakov’s novella nor its film screenplay, and no source in Dostoevsky was ever produced (Fakenews.pl ↗).
Quote aggregators reflect the confusion — Goodreads ↗ lists the line under “Anonymus,” not Dostoevsky.
source.excerptNote: The line has no known author. Early Russian versions circulated as a meme paired with a still of Professor Preobrazhensky from the 1988 Soviet film of Bulgakov’s Heart of a Dog — but the words appear in neither Bulgakov’s novella nor its screenplay.

source.rightsNote: The wording has no identifiable author or source work, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. It is a modern, anonymous internet-era text — not a documented line from any pre-1931 (or any) published work by Dostoevsky.

author.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
author.heading: The author who didn’t write it
author.bio: Fyodor Dostoevsky was the Russian novelist behind Crime and Punishment, The Idiot, Demons and The Brothers Karamazov, works celebrated for their psychological depth and moral seriousness. His fame as a diagnostician of the modern soul makes him a magnet for invented “prophetic” quotes. This anti-tolerance aphorism — framed to read as a prediction of “cancel culture” — is one such fabrication, found nowhere in his writings.

misattribution.heading: How a meme became a “Dostoevsky” quote
misattribution.intro: The line reads like a warning about modern tolerance and free speech — a theme that fits 2020s online argument far better than 19th-century Russia. That anachronism, plus a famous stern face attached to it, is exactly why it spread.

context.heading: Why the fake sticks
lead: The aphorism flatters whoever shares it — casting them as the “intelligent” person silenced by an age of easily-offended “imbeciles.” Attaching Dostoevsky’s name lends the borrowed authority of a great moralist and reframes a partisan jab as timeless prophecy.

Its spread through anti-vaccine and anti-“cancel-culture” circles in 2021 shows the pattern: a modern grievance is dressed in a 19th-century name so it reads as vindicated by history rather than as a fresh opinion.
context.pull: A modern grievance in a 19th-century coat.
